title: Compute the Parity Bit
statement:
A parity bit is the cheapest error check there is. Add one extra bit chosen
so the total number of set bits comes out even, and a receiver that counts an
odd number back knows -- with no further information -- that something in
transit got corrupted. UART links have used it for decades; it is the whole
idea behind a checksum, reduced to one bit.

## Your function

```
int even_parity(unsigned int value);
```

Return the parity bit that would make `value`'s bit count even if it were
appended: `1` if `value` has an **odd** number of set bits, `0` if it already
has an **even** number (zero counts as even).

`even_parity(0x00000001)` is `1` -- one bit set, which is odd.
`even_parity(0x00000003)` is `0` -- two bits set, which is even.

## A different bit trick to the one you may already know

*Count the Set Bits* solves a similar-looking problem by removing one bit at
a time and counting. That works here too -- compute the population count and
return `count & 1` -- but there is a faster way that never counts anything.

Parity is invariant under **XOR-folding**: XOR the top half of the value into
the bottom half, and the parity of what is left is the same as the parity of
the whole thing, because XOR-ing two bits together is exactly "are these two
different", which is exactly what parity already tracks one bit at a time.
Halve it again, and again, and five folds take 32 bits down to 1.

## Watch out

- The parameter is `unsigned int` so that a right shift is always a **logical**
  shift -- zeros come in from the top, never copies of a sign bit. Keep any
  working variable you introduce unsigned too, for the same reason *Count the
  Set Bits* insists on it.

tests.name: every bit set
tests.description: 32 is even -- and the value most likely to break a fold written with a signed working variable.
